Record each line as its own file named by its number (01.mp4, 12.m4a …); one camera take may cover several lines (01-05.mp4). See RECORDING-SCRIPT.md and demo/README.md. scenes.title: No label on the plate
scenes.text: Three times a day, people living with diabetes make the same decision: what to eat, and how much. A packet of biscuits tells you its sugar. A plate of chicken rice from the hawker centre tells you nothing. There's no label and no serving size, and the carbohydrates hide in the rice, the sauce and the drink on the side.

scenes.title: So people guess
scenes.text: So people guess. They guess what's on the plate, how big the portion is, and what it means for their blood sugar. Mixed dishes are hard to break down, portions change from stall to stall, and logging every meal by hand is tedious, so most people simply stop.

scenes.title: Why it matters
scenes.text: And the stakes are high. The World Health Organization counts about eight hundred and thirty million people living with diabetes. In Singapore it's about one adult in twelve, and without effective prevention, up to a million residents could be living with it by twenty fifty. A national study put the cost of diabetes to Singapore at about one billion dollars in twenty ten, rising to two and a half billion by twenty fifty, most of it lost productivity.

scenes.title: The gap
scenes.text: I know visibility works. After Nutri-Grade labels, household sugar from pre-packed drinks fell by about eighteen percent. But labels stop at the bottle and the box. Food apps help you count calories or search a food list. What's still hard is the moment at the stall: knowing what this plate may do to your glucose, and how sure that estimate is.

scenes.title: What MealSenseAI does
scenes.text: That's the gap MealSenseAI fills. One photo becomes foods, portions and nutrition. The numbers become meaning: glucose impact, glycaemic load, and a practical next step. And every estimate is honest about its uncertainty, so the person stays in control of every number. It works for anyone who wants to understand their food, with or without a health condition: the profile sets the goals, such as weight, heart health or balanced eating. I start with diabetes, because that's where the need is sharpest.

scenes.title: Meet Wei Ming
scenes.text: Let me show you. This is Wei Ming, a fictional user who lives with type two diabetes. His profile sets the context: his condition, his goals and a daily carbohydrate target.

scenes.title: Dashboard
scenes.text: His dashboard shows today against those goals, a week of hawker meals, and where his energy comes from. Every number traces back to a meal he logged.

scenes.title: Capture
scenes.text: It's lunchtime, and he's having chicken rice. One photo from above is enough. Behind the scenes, ten steps run in a moment. The image is checked, each food is located and recognised among three hundred and twenty foods, the portion is estimated, and every item is mapped to a nutrition record.

scenes.title: Review
scenes.text: Each food is numbered on the photo, with its portion, calories and carbohydrates, and an honest range, because a photo can't weigh food. When the model is unsure, it says so and shows its next best guesses. Nothing is saved until Wei Ming confirms it.

scenes.title: Mark a missed food
scenes.text: The model doesn't always see everything. When it misses a food, Wei Ming drags a box around it, with a mouse or a finger, and the model looks at just that part. Once he names a food, MealSenseAI remembers it, and recognises it in his next photos.

scenes.title: What it means
scenes.text: Then the part that matters: what it means. The meal's potential glucose impact and its glycaemic load, with practical tips, like less rice or more vegetables. Chicken rice has no published glycaemic index, so MealSenseAI borrows the value of its main carbohydrate, white rice, and says so. The meal advisory flags where the meal goes past public health reference points, and cites its sources.

scenes.title: Portion simulator
scenes.text: What if he asks for less rice? The portion simulator answers before he eats. Slide the portion down, and the carbohydrates, the glycaemic load and the estimated glucose curve all update. It's labelled as an estimate, never as a measurement.

scenes.title: What if I walk?
scenes.text: And what about a fifteen minute walk after lunch? The forecast compares an afternoon at his desk with the walk, and shows how much of the meal's energy it uses. When he logs his own glucose readings, the estimate adjusts to how his body responds.

scenes.title: Meal Advisor
scenes.text: Questions come up, so there's a Meal Advisor. Wei Ming asks how his week went. The answer is built from his own meals and the food table, and each point shows where it came from. It doesn't invent numbers, it never diagnoses, and it can fix a meal in one tap.

scenes.title: Nutrition Insights
scenes.text: Over time, Nutrition Insights turns meals into trends: carbohydrates, sugar, fibre and sodium, day by day. Habits become visible, and so do the small changes that work.

scenes.title: Pricing
scenes.text: Here's the model from my proposal: freemium, to be tested in my trial. A free tier, to log meals and see their nutrition. The subscription, at three ninety-nine a month in Singapore and two ninety-nine in other ASEAN markets, adds the glucose estimates, the Meal Advisor and the simulators. That's well below AI nutrition apps, which run from about nine to sixty US dollars a month. Later, clinics and employers can offer it to their members.

scenes.title: System design
scenes.text: Now, how it works. MealSenseAI runs as four containers on a single server. The browser talks to one web server, which serves the app and forwards requests to a FastAPI backend. The backend holds the models, the nutrition rules and the Meal Advisor, and keeps everything in PostgreSQL. A small language model runs locally beside it. No paid cloud AI is involved.

scenes.title: The ten-stage pipeline
scenes.text: Every photo goes through ten stages, and each one is visible to the user: capture, preprocessing, detection, classification, portion, nutrition, aggregation, explanation, recommendations, and the editable review. Model outputs, estimates and guidance are labelled differently, so it's always clear which is which.

scenes.title: Recognising the food
scenes.text: Recognition uses EfficientNet-B0, a compact network that runs on an ordinary CPU. I trained it myself, on two public datasets: Food-101 and the Singapore dataset FoodSG-233. Here is how.

scenes.title: Training the model
scenes.text: I started with three hundred and ten thousand images. A checksum audit found two thousand groups of identical files, so I removed forty-one hundred images with conflicting labels or duplicates; no image appears in both training and test. I kept Food-101's official test set and split FoodSG eighty, ten, ten. Training ran in two stages on my own GPU server. First, a new head for three hundred and twenty classes on a frozen backbone. Then the last three blocks as well, with a lower learning rate for the pretrained layers. Each stage took about twenty minutes, and validation macro-F1 rose from fifty-eight to sixty-six percent. On forty-five thousand eight hundred test images it scores seventy-one percent top-one and eighty-six percent top-three. Its confidence tracks its accuracy to within about two percent, which supports the app's thresholds. Exported to ONNX, it gives the same top three as the original, in about twelve milliseconds on a CPU.

scenes.title: Several foods on a plate
scenes.text: Real plates have several foods. A YOLO segmentation model proposes regions, and each region is classified. On a hundred multi-food test plates, detection reached seventy-five percent precision and sixty-eight percent recall, at about a quarter of a second per plate. That's why the review stays human in the loop: a correction is one tap, or one dragged box.

scenes.title: Portions, nutrition and glycaemic load
scenes.text: Each class maps to a nutrition record: two hundred and forty-seven exactly, sixty-six through the nearest food, and seven left for the user to choose. Portions come from typical servings, or from the food's area against the plate, always with an uncertainty band. Glycaemic load uses published GI values, and where a dish has none, fixed rules borrow the value of its staple. That covers seventy-eight more foods.

scenes.title: The glucose estimate
scenes.text: The glucose estimate is a one-compartment mass-balance model. Glucose from the meal appears over time, is cleared at a rate set by the person's condition, and is used faster by working muscle during activity. It's anchored to typical glucose tolerance results, and after three meals with before and after readings, it calibrates to the person's own response.

scenes.title: A grounded Meal Advisor
scenes.text: The Meal Advisor is grounded by design. A rule engine writes the answer from the user's own data first. The local language model, Qwen two point five, only rewords it, and a validator checks every number and food name against the facts before anything is shown. If the check fails, the rule-based answer is used. On thirty-eight test questions, covering arithmetic, safety and prompt injection, every answer passed, with no unsupported claims.

scenes.title: Learning safely
scenes.text: It also learns safely. A food the user names is stored as a fingerprint and matched by cosine similarity, so it's recognised next time without retraining. Photos are shared for training only with consent. Each one is screened for poisoning patterns, and a new model must pass a gate on a fixed test set, then run in shadow mode, before it can go live.

scenes.title: Configuring the models
scenes.text: Every model is configured in the admin area, without changing code. For recognition, the thresholds are set here, and the calibration results back them: below point two a guess is not added, and a plate region below point four five is shown as unidentified. The personal food memory works like an embedding: each food a user names is stored as the classifier's own three-hundred-and-twenty-value output, and a new photo reuses that name when the cosine similarity is at least point seven. For the local language model I choose the model, here Qwen 2.5 with one and a half billion parameters on Ollama, a temperature of point one for consistent wording, and time limits after which the rule engine answers instead. Its prompts are versioned, so I can change one and roll it back. I benchmarked it against the rules: it was good at rewording and weak on facts, so it only rewords, and every output is checked.

scenes.title: Tested and deployable
scenes.text: Quality is tested end to end, against a real database and a real browser: sixty-four automated tests, plus an acceptance run from sign-up to saved meal, which also passes with no internet, and keeps every record across a restart. It deploys with one Docker Compose command on a CPU server.

scenes.title: MealSenseAI
scenes.text: Diabetes is managed one meal at a time, and so is everyday healthy eating. Most of those meals have no label. MealSenseAI puts the information on the plate, at the moment the choice is made. MealSenseAI. Understand your food. Make healthier choices.
